title: Planning a team Christmas dinner with a private chef

body_markdown:
A good team Christmas dinner starts with a usable brief. Decide who is coming, where the meal will happen and the total budget before discussing dishes. A chef can then propose something that suits the room, the timetable and the group.


We looked at the team and work Christmas dinners booked through yhangry over the last two Decembers to show what they cost, when they happen and how they come together.


## What a team Christmas dinner costs


The typical team Christmas dinner on yhangry came to around £940 in total, for a group of 12. The middle half landed between about £600 and £1,560. Per head, that worked out at around £62, a little less than a typical December dinner party (£73), with team groups usually larger.


Set a budget that covers the whole evening. Separate the food and chef service from venue hire, drinks, equipment and any transport. Then decide whether you want a seated meal, a sharing dinner or a standing reception with substantial food, because each needs different staffing and space.


Give the chef the expected headcount and an honest spending limit. Say whether you need an invoice for the company and who can approve the booking. If several people need to sign off, build that into your timetable rather than holding a chef’s date on an assumption.


## When team dinners happen


Team dinners run on a different calendar from other December parties. Nearly nine in ten were held on a weekday, most often a Thursday or Friday, while most other December dinners fell at the weekend. They were also booked closer to the date: typically about three weeks ahead, against nearly five weeks for other December dinners.


Short notice can work. One London office booked its chef two days before its Christmas party. But it leaves little time to agree the menu and venue details, so send your brief as soon as you have a date and a rough headcount.


## Choose the venue first


An office dinner saves everyone another journey, but the kitchen may be designed for making tea rather than serving a meal. A rented house or event space raises different questions about access, permissions and equipment. Check the venue before you commit to a format.


Over the last two Decembers, about half of the team dinners on yhangry took place in an office or rented space rather than someone’s home. Some of those offices had little more than a microwave and a small hob, and the dinners still worked because the chef knew in advance and planned around it.


## Match the menu to the event


If the point is a relaxed evening with the team, sharing dishes suit the room. If you are hosting clients or presenting awards, a plated meal gives you clearer breaks in the programme. Ask how speeches or presentations will affect service, especially for dishes that need to be served straight away.


Collect dietary requirements through one organiser. Pass the relevant details to the chef in good time and arrange a direct conversation where needed. Nobody should have to explain an allergy for the first time as their plate arrives.


## Check the venue with the chef


Share photos of the food preparation area, cooking facilities and dining space. Confirm loading access, parking, lifts, waste arrangements and when the chef can arrive and leave. Ask whether the venue needs documents such as proof of insurance, and agree how these will be supplied.


Tell the chef what tableware the venue has. Offices often have plates and cutlery but nothing to serve or carve with, so ask the chef to bring serving dishes and utensils if you need them. If cooking facilities are limited, let the chef suggest a menu that can be prepared ahead and finished on site. Don’t assume a portable appliance solves every access, electrical or permission issue.


## Build a running order around service


A simple evening might be drinks on arrival, then dinner, with speeches between agreed courses. Treat that as a starting point to discuss with your chef rather than a fixed timetable. Decide who will welcome the chef, who will direct any waiting staff and who can make a call if the schedule changes.


## A real office Christmas party: 26 guests, no kitchen


Last December, a London office booked[Chef John L](https://yhangry.com/booking/chef/john-l/) just two days before its Christmas party. There were 26 guests, including some plus ones, seated along one long table in the office.


**The brief.** The organiser was upfront about the limits: no cooking facilities beyond a microwave and a small hob. The office had its own plates and cutlery but needed the chef to bring serving and carving equipment. There was no need for him to stay once the food was served.


**The plan.** John designed a Christmas menu with a twist, from hors d’oeuvres to dessert, and prepared everything in advance. At the office he set it out as a sharing spread. The menu covered vegetarian, coeliac and halal guests.


**The cost.** The total came to £784, about £30 a head, with ingredients included.


**The result.** The organiser said everything ran smoothly, the food was delicious and varied, and called it great value. They rated the evening five stars.

The lesson for other organisers: be honest about the venue. A clear description of what the office did and didn’t have let the chef plan a menu that worked, even at short notice.


## Make booking and follow-up straightforward


Before paying, confirm the final quote, staffing, payment schedule, cancellation terms and the deadline for changes. On yhangry, events booked more than 30 days ahead are secured with a deposit and the balance is taken 30 days before. Team dinners are typically booked about three weeks out, so many organisers pay in full when they book. Full details are on our[payments page](https://yhangry.com/blog/?p=12953) .


Share the agreed arrival details with whoever manages the venue. After the dinner, ask the team what worked and keep the brief for next year.


**Planning this year’s team dinner?**[Send yhangry your brief](https://yhangry.com/) with your date, postcode, guest count, budget and venue details. The more precise the brief, the more useful the chef’s proposal will be.


FAQs


How much does a private chef cost for a work Christmas dinner?


On yhangry, the typical team Christmas dinner came to around £940 for 12 people, or about £62 a head. The middle half of bookings fell between about £600 and £1,560.


Can a private chef cook in an office with no kitchen?


Yes, with planning. Tell the chef exactly what the venue has. One London office with only a microwave and a small hob had a sharing spread for 26, prepared in advance and set out on site.


How far ahead should we book a chef for a team Christmas party?


Team dinners on yhangry were typically booked about three weeks ahead. Last-minute bookings do happen, but booking earlier gives you more time to agree the menu and venue logistics.


Which day do most teams choose for their Christmas dinner?


Nearly nine in ten team dinners on yhangry were held on a weekday, most often a Thursday or Friday.


Can the chef cater for different dietary requirements


Yes. Collect requirements through one organiser and share them with the chef before the menu is agreed. Arrange a direct conversation for any allergy.
